hints: Look carefully at the starting conditions: you mix a fixed amount of substrate with enzyme at time 0, then leave it until it is complete. When is there the most substrate available to collide with enzyme?
Remember that reaction rate depends on successful enzyme-substrate collisions, so think about what happens to substrate concentration and rate as substrate is used up to zero.
walkthrough:
**Picture what is in the tube at the start**

At time 0 you have just mixed all your substrate with enzyme. Substrate concentration is at its highest, so collisions and enzyme-substrate complexes form most frequently.

That means the rate of reaction starts at its maximum value.

**Follow what happens as time passes**

As the reaction proceeds, substrate is converted to product and is not replaced. Less substrate means fewer collisions per unit time, so the rate steadily falls.

This is a closed system with a fixed amount of substrate, so the fall is continuous.

**Finish when the reaction is complete**

The question says the reaction is left until it was complete. That means all substrate is used up, so no more enzyme-substrate complexes can form.

Rate must finish at zero and stay there, which matches only graph C: high at start, curving down to zero.

options.A: Shows rate increasing with time, but substrate is being used up not added, so collisions and rate cannot keep increasing.
options.B: Shows rate rising then staying high, but with no new substrate the rate cannot be maintained, it must fall to zero when substrate runs out.
options.C: Correct, rate is highest at the start when substrate is plentiful, then decreases as substrate is used up, reaching zero when the reaction is complete.
options.D: Shows rate starting low, rising to a peak then falling, which fits an optimum curve like temperature or pH, not a time course with fixed substrate.
